title: Probation Prep Pack
description: The composite playbook for the final 21 days of a PM's probation. Four sub-artefacts: a self-assessment template, the agenda for the pre-review 1:1 you book a week before the formal review, an evidence portfolio template, and a worked example of an actual probation review conversation. The voice across all four is calibrated against probation anxiety — honesty over reassurance, calibration over comfort. This is the playbook the user takes into the review.

# Probation Prep Pack — Project Manager
_Use the four sub-artefacts below in this order: self-assessment first (to know what you have), pre-review 1:1 second (to pull clarity from your manager), evidence portfolio third (to assemble receipts), conversation playbook last (to rehearse)._

## Sub-artefact 1: Self-Assessment

One page. Three columns. Filled in honestly. Not a sales pitch.

| Delivered | Learned | Want next |
|-----------|---------|-----------|
_Three to five items in each column. Specific. Each item names a programme, a date, a number, or a person._

## Sub-artefact 2: Pre-Review 1:1 Agenda

The meeting you book a week before the formal review. Thirty minutes. Framing:

> 'I want to make sure I'm walking into our review well-prepared. Can we talk about what good looks like at the end of this probation?'

Note what changed in that sentence. Not 'what do you want me to do' (defensive) — 'what does good look like' (forward, framing your role rather than your tasks).

### Agenda

1. **My read of the last ninety days** (3 minutes). One paragraph. Specific. Not exhaustive.
2. **What I think went well and what was hard** (5 minutes). Two of each. Concrete.
3. **Your read** (15 minutes). The bulk of the meeting. Listen.
4. **What 'continued' looks like to you** (5 minutes). Ask explicitly.
5. **What you'd like me to bring to the formal review** (2 minutes).

## Sub-artefact 3: Evidence Portfolio

_Not a CV. A working file of three to five named things that demonstrate the hire is working out._

| Item | Date | Anonymised description | What it demonstrates |
|------|------|-----------------------|----------------------|
|      |      |                       |                      |

_The anonymisation column is the discipline. 'Negotiated the slip on the migration programme' is recognisable; 'led the conversation when a critical-path delivery dependency was at risk' lands without exposing your sponsor or your team._

## Sub-artefact 4: The Conversation Playbook

_See the worked example below — an actual probation review conversation, annotated turn by turn._

worked_examples.content_md:
# The Probation Review Conversation — Worked Example

_Setting: Bethan Lloyd-Owen (Programme Director, hiring manager) and Adekunle Bello (PM). Day 88. Thirty minutes booked. Two programmes delivered, one with a documented slip, one stakeholder complaint, one strong sponsor reference, one near-miss saved (the lead dev retention)._

---

**Bethan:** Thanks for the pack. So — how do you think it's gone?

_[**Adekunle's silent thought:** This is the only question that matters. The answer I give in the next thirty seconds frames the whole conversation. Don't open with the sales pitch.]_

**Adekunle:** Three things, if that's useful. The migration programme landed three weeks late, which I flagged in week 5; the customer-portal programme is on track for September with the change-requests we agreed; and the thing I'm most proud of is the retro in week 8 with Lewis's team — that conversation kept him on the team.

_[**Annotation:** Opens with three specifics, ordered by what's hardest to acknowledge. Most candidates open with the wins; Adekunle opens with the slip because Bethan already knows about it and acknowledging it first removes its power as a negotiating chip Bethan would otherwise have to play.]_

**Bethan:** The migration slip — talk me through that.

**Adekunle:** I should have flagged it three days earlier than I did. I knew the integration window was tightening by Wednesday; I waited until Friday. By Friday it was a meeting; on Wednesday it would have been a Slack message. That's the thing I'd do differently.

_[**Annotation:** Specific, dated, named the precise corrective action. Not 'I'd communicate better' (a category, not a behaviour). Bethan now knows Adekunle has actually thought about this rather than rehearsed an answer.]_

**Bethan:** And the stakeholder thing — Tom Reilly's email.

_[**Adekunle's silent thought:** Tom escalated to her boss. This is the hard one. Don't be defensive; don't apologise excessively either.]_

**Adekunle:** Tom and I had a hard conversation in week 6. I think I handled the substance — we got to a working agreement on the data extract — but I handled the manner badly. I cut him off twice in that meeting; I shouldn't have. I went back to him in week 7 to acknowledge it directly. He's still in my Friday email distribution.

_[**Annotation:** Names the specific behaviour ('cut him off twice'). Doesn't blame Tom. Mentions the repair conversation. Adekunle is not over-apologising and not under-acknowledging.]_

**Bethan:** Mei-Lin says you're sharper than the last three PMs we hired.

**Adekunle:** That's a generous read. I think Mei-Lin and I clicked early because I held a number on a team estimate — the integration estimate in week 6. She tests new PMs on whether they'll cave under direct pressure. I held the number because the team had done the analysis honestly; it wasn't bravery on my part, it was the work being right.

_[**Annotation:** Receives the compliment without deflecting it OR over-claiming it. Reframes Mei-Lin's read as situational, not characterological — which Bethan will trust more than 'oh that's just because I'm good with sponsors.']_

**Bethan:** OK. So — what are you most worried about going into next quarter?

_[**Adekunle's silent thought:** This is the question Bethan was always going to ask. The answer matters more than anything I've said so far.]_

**Adekunle:** The thing I haven't done yet is run a programme through a vendor crisis. The Synth Logistics risk on the portal is the closest I've come, and I've been able to manage it as a tracked risk — I haven't had to actually call the contingency. If a vendor went down on me in Q3, I think I'd handle it; I'm not certain I'd handle it well. That's the gap.

_[**Annotation:** One worry, specific, named, with a self-assessment of confidence level. Not 'nothing really' (false confidence). Not five worries (panic). This is the answer that distinguishes a confirmed-but-watched PM from a confirmed-and-trusted PM. Bethan will sit with this answer.]_

**Bethan:** Yeah, that's fair. The Synth Logistics call is going to come in the next six months — I'm thinking about how we partner you with Mei-Lin on that one when it does. 

_[**Annotation:** Bethan has just told Adekunle two things. One: she's already thinking about Adekunle's next quarter. Two: she's thinking about partnering Adekunle with the sponsor who likes him. That's a green-light read.]_

**Adekunle:** That would be useful. Can I ask — what's the one thing you'd want me to be doing differently in the next ninety days?

_[**Annotation:** Closes with a question that demonstrates thinking past confirmation. Not 'is there anything I should improve?' (passive). The specific 'one thing' makes it answerable.]_

**Bethan:** Honestly, you've earned the right to lead a portfolio-board presentation without me in the room by Christmas. I want you to want that. 

---

_Adekunle walked out of the room without a confirmed-yes — Bethan ended the meeting with 'we'll talk on Day 90' — but with a near-certainty. Bethan named what 'continued' looks like: portfolio-board presentations independent of the Director by Christmas. That's a forward-looking benchmark, not a backward-looking grade._

annotations.note: Self-assessment is not a CV. The discipline is honesty in the 'Learned' column. Most candidates fill 'Delivered' generously, 'Learned' thinly, 'Want next' aspirationally. The Bethan-quality reviewer will read 'Learned' most carefully — that's where evidence of self-awareness lives.

The pre-review 1:1 framing — 'what does good look like' — is the most useful sentence in this entire playbook. The phrasing pulls clarity from the manager rather than feedback. Feedback is backward-looking; clarity is forward-looking. The reframe matters more than the meeting itself.

Evidence portfolio is three to five items, not fifteen. Three-to-five is the band where the candidate can actually narrate each item with specifics. A portfolio of fifteen items becomes a list; a portfolio of three becomes a story.

The worked conversation is the artefact that makes this pack a signature playbook. The annotations are turn-by-turn editorial commentary — what's happening below the surface of each line. Read it twice.

common_mistakes: Self-assessment written as a sales pitch. The 'Learned' column ends up with one item ('learned a lot') and the 'Delivered' column ends up with ten. Reviewers read the imbalance immediately and discount the whole document.
Pre-review 1:1 not booked, or booked too late. The whole point is to get clarity a week BEFORE the formal review. A 1:1 booked the day before the review becomes the review.

Evidence portfolio not anonymised. 'Tom from Reilly Industries escalated to Bethan' is recognisable to anyone with two minutes of internal context. 'A stakeholder escalated; I handled the substance well and the manner badly, then went back to repair' is the same content, professionally framed.
Reviewing the conversation playbook once and assuming you've absorbed it. The annotations matter. Read the worked example twice; the second read is where the editorial moves become learnable.

Treating the formal review as a presentation. It's a conversation. The candidate who presents their pack in the room is the candidate who has not done the homework — the pack should have done the presenting in advance, leaving the room for the conversation itself.
Bringing five worries to the 'what are you most worried about next quarter' question. One is honesty; five is panic. Pick the one that is most accurate.
variant_patterns: Extended-probation variant: if the user's probation outcome was 'extended', the conversation playbook becomes a different worked example — the conversation where the user pulls 'what specifically would land as continued in the next 30 days' from the manager. The self-assessment template is unchanged.

Cross-functional review variant (multiple reviewers): the pre-review 1:1 becomes 1:1s with each reviewer separately, in the week before the formal review. The evidence portfolio item-count grows by one for each additional reviewer.

Non-standard probation length (6 months instead of 90 days): the pack structure is unchanged. The Probation Mode in FirstNinety activates 21 days before whatever review date applies, regardless of length.
